source.title: Attention as a Routing Graph: Live Circuit Extraction from a Single Forward Pass

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether an extracted circuit-like subgraph causally affects IOI using a different method from the original head-circuit analysis: single-pass routing-graph extraction followed by edge ablation.
record.gate_note: The IOI edge-ablation results are recorded. The induction results and the induction-only parameter and prompt variations do not bear on the IOI claim versions. The paper reports the IOI results as name logit-difference drops; it does not report the exact 26-head circuit or its stated head-class roles.
record.test_reason: The study uses IOI as a benchmark with a known circuit to validate its own single-pass routing-sketch method. It reports only how much ablating its extracted token-to-token edges hurts the name logit-difference compared with random edge sets. For IOI it never compares its edges with the 26-head circuit, its head classes, backup heads or the original criteria. Head-overlap checks are reported for induction only. Its results show the method's own performance, not whether any IOI version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors conclude that a one-forward routing sketch plus an ablation check carries real causal signal on induction and IOI, with 'honest partial recovery'. They say it is not a complete circuit discovery method. They note that uniform random controls remove less attention mass, so a mass-matched control would shrink the gaps by an unmeasured amount.
record.recipe_differences: The study ranks token-to-token attention edges from a single forward pass using attention weight times value-vector norm, then ablates the selected edges and compares score drops with random edge sets. It does not reproduce the original head-class circuit analysis or its faithfulness, completeness and minimality tests.
record.method_sensitivity: For GPT-2 Small induction, the paper reports that a walk with k=5 is unreliable, k≥10 is stable, harsh score thresholds and late layers alone fail, and early layers recover most of the gap. It says changing the induction prompt template or adding filler sentences does not kill the gap. These variations are not reported for IOI.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating single-pass routing edges selected by attention weight times value norm cuts the IOI name logit-difference far more than random same-size edge sets. Gaps are +5.16 (GPT-2 Small), +3.05 (GPT-2 Medium) and +5.63 (Pythia-410M). The authors say part of each gap is an attention-mass effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A cheap attention-routing sketch from one forward pass captures causally relevant IOI routes beyond random edges, across small open models.

record.problems: For IOI, the random control is not attention-mass-matched: the selected set removes more attention mass, and the authors say an unmeasured mass-matched control could shrink the gaps. The IOI tests use 100 prompts per model. The paper reports score drops rather than a direct IOI accuracy measure.
record.rows_left_out: No IOI results were left out. Induction results and induction-only parameter and prompt variations were omitted because they do not test the IOI claim versions.

untested.parts: The 26 heads, the seven classes and their roles, and faithfulness, completeness and minimality are not examined for IOI.
Name-mover ablation and backup-head self-repair are not tested.
IOI head classes and roles in GPT-2 Medium and Pythia-410M are not identified, and component reuse is not tested.
The extracted IOI edges are not compared with the known IOI circuit, so recovery of the same circuit is not assessed.
The ablation type, metric and prompt distribution are not varied for the IOI circuit. The mass confound concerns the study's own random control, not the IOI circuit's faithfulness.
Name orders, templates and more names are not tested for IOI. Template and filler variations are reported for induction only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification and its V1/V5 labels are not justified. For IOI the paper never maps its edges onto the known heads; overlap with known heads is shown only for induction (Section 3.3). The V5 limits_scope label conflated a confound in the study's own control with sensitivity of the IOI circuit's evaluation. All three rows are reclassified as method-performance results with no version links.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test the specified 26 attention heads, their seven classes or stated roles, or the original faithfulness, completeness and minimality criteria.
It does not ablate the main name-mover heads or test backup-head self-repair.
IOI is evaluated on other models, but the study does not test whether the same head classes and roles carry IOI there or whether components are reused for other tasks.
It does not compare circuit-finding methods, ablation types or metrics to determine whether they recover essentially the same circuit.
The study discusses a mass confound in its IOI evaluation, but does not report a mass-matched IOI control or vary IOI ablation types, metrics or prompt distributions.
Prompt-template and filler variations are reported for induction, not IOI; the study does not test IOI across name orders, templates or more names.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.operation_detail: Ablated the extracted routing edges by turning off their attention weights and renormalizing the remaining weights; compared with ten random edge sets of the same size.

conditions.value: 10 edge sets of the same size

rows.measure: Mean drop in name logit-difference; paired gap between extracted-edge and random-edge drops
rows.uncertainty: ± values are one standard deviation across prompts. The paper says the 95% bootstrap CI for the gap excludes 0 and Wilcoxon p<10^-10, but does not give this cell's exact CI in the text.
rows.note: The extracted edges have a much larger reported score drop than random edges. This is evidence about the study's routing-edge sketch, not the specified 26-head circuit. The authors note that the extracted set removes more attention mass than the random control.
rows.check: The row measures the study's own extracted routing edges against random edges, not the 26-head circuit or its classes. Its gap (+5.16) evaluates the method, so it bears on no version. The state 'partial' against V1/V5 has no basis.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Medium
rows.operation_detail: Ablated the extracted routing edges by turning off their attention weights and renormalizing the remaining weights; compared with ten random edge sets of the same size.

conditions.value: 10 edge sets of the same size

rows.measure: Mean drop in name logit-difference; paired gap between extracted-edge and random-edge drops
rows.uncertainty: ± values are one standard deviation across prompts; 95% bootstrap CI for the gap [+2.63, +3.46]; Wilcoxon p<10^-10.
rows.note: The study reports 12/100 examples where the extracted-edge ablation drop was no greater than the random-edge drop. The paper also notes the extracted set removes more attention mass than the random control.
rows.check: Same issue: this is a method-validation result (gap +3.05, 12/100 fails) for the study's own edge sets. It does not bear on the IOI circuit, its sensitivity to ablation or metric choices, or cross-model head roles.

rows.subject: Pythia-410M
rows.operation_detail: Ablated the extracted routing edges by turning off their attention weights and renormalizing the remaining weights; compared with ten random edge sets of the same size.

conditions.value: 10 edge sets of the same size

rows.measure: Mean drop in name logit-difference; paired gap between extracted-edge and random-edge drops
rows.uncertainty: ± values are one standard deviation across prompts. The paper says the 95% bootstrap CI for the gap excludes 0 and Wilcoxon p<10^-10, but does not give this cell's exact CI in the text.
rows.note: The authors describe this IOI result as essentially clean, with 0/100 examples where the extracted-edge drop was no greater than the random-edge drop. The paper notes the extracted set removes more attention mass than the random control.
rows.check: Same issue: this is a method-validation result (gap +5.63, 0/100 fails). Running Pythia does not test V3, because no head classes or roles are identified for IOI.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: IOI routing-edge ablations on GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 Medium and Pythia-410M
reader_labels.reason: In all three models, ablating the study's extracted edges produced a larger name-logit-difference drop than random same-size edge sets (ioi-small, ioi-medium, ioi-pythia). This supports causal relevance of an extracted IOI route, not the specified head classes or criteria.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The study tests its own edge sets rather than the named 26-head circuit and states that its sketch is not a complete circuit atlas; the results therefore do not establish the claimed head classes or completeness and minimality (ioi-small, ioi-medium, ioi-pythia).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: IOI edge-ablation comparisons across the three tested models
reader_labels.reason: The authors state that the extracted sets remove more attention mass than uniformly sampled random sets, so part of the measured gap may be a mass effect; they did not measure how much a mass-matched control would shrink it (ioi-small, ioi-medium, ioi-pythia).
